The word for the new birth is not really a birth at all, but is the Greek word for change. The big metaphor of this missive by Paul is the idea of what happens when organisms come together – the parts that make up our bodies are joined together as one.
That’s why it’s not a big deal to eat vegetables. But when we join ourselves to a member of the opposite sex the body of these individuals becomes that of one member.
This is seen in a broader way and is best explained by the image of a puzzle. The puzzle starts as individual pieces, each one looking similar but unique and that have the same basic geometric shapes and some color likeness from one piece to another. But this is all limited. But once we start to reveal the puzzle, we discover that the single pieces join together for a higher purpose. The individual pattern and shape likenesses of these single pieces look identical by themselves, but as they become a part of the big picture they are distinct pieces of a much bigger whole.
Over time, the individual can take on and identify with a unique single instance that is different and unlike any of the others. But just as I encourage our kids to discover the unique piece, I also hope that they’ll also enjoy the big picture. They might be able to enjoy the bodies as they are, but the entire force becomes much stronger

No Accidental Zombies is an unusual picture book in that it’s really two very different stories in one. As a picture book, this modelling of a quite clear idea is useful, but the topic is something which might evade some younger readers.
